# Results — Study 66 (Inverted): the yield curve as an equity-downturn signal, 1985–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly **10-year (^TNX)** and **13-week
(^IRX)** Treasury yields and the **S&P 500 (^GSPC)**, Yahoo, 1985–2026. Curve slope = 10y − 3m; <0 ⇒
inverted. Inputs fingerprint `e68e9ffd8fbd`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `FRAGILE` · "Forecasts equity downturns"? `CONFIRMED`

The inverted yield curve is a `REAL` macro signal, and a strong one: after the curve inverts, the next
**18 months of equities averaged +1.0% vs +15.8%** in normal times, and the next **24 months −8.7% vs
+21.7%** — a 30-point gap. That is `CONFIRMED`. But it is `FRAGILE` to *trade*: inversions are rare (~5%
of months), the lead time to the downturn is **long and variable** (6–24 months), and in the *near* term
markets often keep rising — at the 12-month horizon the gap is only −4.2%. As a recession barometer it's
one of the best there is; as a market-timing trigger it would have you out of stocks for a year or more
of gains before the fall.

## Data stamp

- **Series**: ^TNX (10y) / ^IRX (3m) / ^GSPC, monthly, 1985–2026, fingerprint `e68e9ffd8fbd`

## Equity returns after an inverted vs a normal curve

| forward horizon | after **inverted** | after **normal** | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 months | +6.1% | +10.3% | −4.2% |
| 18 months | **+1.0%** | +15.8% | **−14.8%** |
| 24 months | **−8.7%** | +21.7% | **−30.4%** |

The signal *strengthens with horizon*: an inversion barely dents the next year (markets often climb into
the recession), but the 18–24-month window — when the recession actually bites — is flat-to-negative
against a +16–22% normal backdrop. This is the textbook recession lead, and it's economically enormous.

## Why it's `REAL` but `FRAGILE` to trade

1. **The lead is long and variable.** An inversion has preceded essentially every modern recession, but
   anywhere from 6 to 24 months ahead. A rule that sells on inversion sits out, on average, a year of
   gains first (the 12-month gap is only −4.2%).
2. **It's rare.** ~5% of months are inverted (a few dozen observations), so the *timing* sample is thin
   even as the *economic* signal is robust.
3. **Near-term it can be wrong-footed.** Markets frequently melt up after inversion (1998, 2006, 2019,
   2023) before the eventual drop — punishing an early exit.

## The honest takeaway

The inverted yield curve `CONFIRMED`-ly forecasts weak equity returns at the 18–24-month horizon (+1% /
−9% vs +16% / +22% normally) — a `REAL`, economically large macro signal, the best recession barometer
there is. But it's `FRAGILE` as a *timer*: rare, slow, variable-lag, and near-term unreliable. Use it to
set the *odds* and your *risk posture*, not to flip a switch on a date.
